questions.q: What anti-pattern does the original `estimate_ghz_fidelity(n_qubits, shots, use_real_hardware=False)` use to select its backend, and what does the lab replace it with?
options: A boolean flag branching inside the function; replaced with injecting a QuantumBackend instance as a parameter
A global variable; replaced with an environment variable
A command-line argument; replaced with a config file only
There was no backend-selection problem in the original function
questions.explain: The original function used a use_real_hardware boolean to branch between AerSimulator and real-hardware code inline. The lab replaces this with dependency injection (Lesson 11), passing a QuantumBackend instance as a parameter instead.

questions.q: After the refactor, which extracted function can be tested with a hand-constructed counts dictionary and zero quantum execution at all?
options: build_ghz_circuit, because it never touches counts
run_and_get_counts, because it directly calls the backend
fidelity_from_counts, because it's pure analysis logic taking counts, n_qubits, and shots as plain data
estimate_ghz_fidelity, because it's the top-level composed function
questions.explain: fidelity_from_counts only operates on a plain dict of counts plus two integers -- no circuit, no backend, no execution -- so it can be tested with entirely synthetic input data, which was impossible in the original tangled function.

questions.q: How does the lab verify that `build_ghz_circuit` is behavior-preserving relative to the original inline circuit-building code?
options: By assuming it must be correct since the code looks similar
By asserting the extracted function's gate sequence (circuit.data) matches what the original inline code would have produced
By running it on real IBM hardware and comparing cost
By checking that the function's name contains the word 'build'
questions.explain: The lab writes a construction test asserting the gate_names sequence from build_ghz_circuit matches the structure the original inline code produced -- a concrete, checkable claim rather than an assumption.

questions.q: Why does the lab deliberately NOT add an SDK-adapter layer (Lesson 12) during this refactor?
options: Because SDK adapters are impossible to implement
Because this project only targets Qiskit-compatible backends, and adding that layer with no second SDK in sight would be the speculative over-engineering Lesson 12 warned against
Because SDK adapters are only for statistical tests, not architecture
Because Lesson 12 was about documentation, not architecture
questions.explain: The lab explicitly stops at backend abstraction (Lesson 11) rather than adding a multi-SDK adapter layer, since there's no actual second-SDK requirement -- directly applying Lesson 12's warning against building abstraction before it's needed.

questions.q: According to the lab's architecture review checklist, what should be true of each function extracted during the refactor?
options: Each extracted function should have an independent test that doesn't require the other extracted functions
Each extracted function must call every other extracted function to be valid
Extracted functions should be merged back together before deployment
Only the top-level composed function needs any test coverage
questions.explain: The checklist specifically requires that each extracted function (construction, execution, analysis) has its own independent test -- exactly what made fidelity_from_counts testable with synthetic data and build_ghz_circuit testable with no backend.
